title: Putting Evidence Together
theme: Task verbs for synthesis and critique
objectives: I can use task verbs such as synthesize, corroborate, and contextualize to describe what I am doing with evidence.
I can tell a postulate from a hypothesis and an extrapolation from a summary.
I can juxtapose two sources to show what they share and where they differ.
I can use the endings -ize, -ate, and -ify to recognize verbs.
rationale: Grade 8 prompts rarely ask students to retell; they ask them to combine sources, judge them, and project beyond them. This unit adds ten higher-level task verbs to the grade 7 analysis set so students can name the thinking a prompt asks for before they begin. The words fall into three moves: building an idea (hypothesize, postulate, extrapolate), checking it (corroborate, contextualize, juxtapose), and putting it into words (synthesize, delineate, articulate, exemplify). Because the grade 8 words are mostly Latin-derived verbs ending in -ize, -ate, and -ify, the unit also trains students to recognize verb endings. Students will see these verbs again on science investigations, history document tasks, and every constructed-response prompt for the rest of the year.

words.def: To combine ideas or information from several sources into one new, connected understanding.
words.ex: To answer the essay prompt, Lena had to synthesize a diary, a map, and a newspaper article.
words.ex2: The scientist's report synthesized ten years of studies into one clear explanation.
words.nonExample: Listing what three sources say, one after another, without connecting them is not synthesizing.

apps.academic: When a prompt says synthesize, write one claim that draws on all the sources instead of summarizing each in turn.
apps.spoken: Let's synthesize what we learned from both groups before we decide.
apps.writing: Use synthesize when you combine sources into an idea that none of them states alone.

cloze.s: To ___ the three articles, the student wrote one paragraph explaining what they all agreed on and where they differed.

cloze2.s: Good historians ___ many fragments of evidence into a single story that makes sense.

misuse.s: She synthesized the sources by copying one article word for word and ignoring the other two.
misuse.why: To synthesize is to combine several sources; copying one and ignoring the rest does not.

visual.alt: Puzzle pieces fitting together on top of a stack of books.

words.frame: To synthesize these sources, I would say that ___.

words.def: To suggest or assume that something is true, as a starting point for an argument or theory.
words.ex: Dr. Rao postulated that sleep helps the brain sort new memories, and then designed an experiment to test the idea.
words.ex2: Philosophers sometimes postulate an unseen force first and look for evidence afterward.
words.nonExample: Reporting a number that you have already measured is not postulating.

apps.academic: A writer who postulates an explanation must be ready to support it with evidence later in the paper.
apps.spoken: I'd postulate that the bus was late because of the rain, but I haven't checked.
apps.writing: Use postulate for an assumption you put forward as a starting point, not as a proven fact.

cloze.s: Before the experiment, the team ___ that warmer water would make the seeds sprout faster.

cloze2.s: Given the footprints by the window, the detective ___ that the visitor had come in through the back way.

misuse.s: The scientist postulated her theory only after the experiment had already proved it beyond any doubt.
misuse.why: To postulate is to propose a starting assumption before proof, not after it.

visual.alt: A lightbulb above a notebook with a question written in it.

words.frame: I postulate that ___, but I would need ___ to prove it.

words.def: To support a claim or account by giving evidence from another independent source.
words.ex: A second eyewitness corroborated the first witness's account of the accident.
words.ex2: The diary entry corroborates what the town's newspaper reported that week.
words.nonExample: Repeating the same claim louder does not corroborate it.
words.rel: backing up with a second source

apps.academic: In history, a claim is stronger when at least two independent sources corroborate it.
apps.spoken: Can anyone corroborate what he said about the game?
apps.writing: Use corroborate when a second, separate source supports the first; it needs independent evidence.

cloze.s: The security video ___ her story that she had been in the library at noon.

cloze2.s: A single post proves little, so reporters look for a second source to ___ it before printing the story.

misuse.s: The new evidence corroborated the claim by showing that it was false.
misuse.why: To corroborate is to support; evidence showing the claim is false contradicts it.

visual.alt: Two separate documents linked together by a check mark.

words.frame: A second source that corroborates ___ is ___.

words.def: To use known facts or patterns to make a careful estimate about something not yet known.
words.ex: From last year's rainfall records, the engineers extrapolated how much water the reservoir would hold in spring.
words.ex2: A reader can extrapolate from the first three chapters that the narrator will keep avoiding the truth.
words.nonExample: Reading a number that is printed on a chart is not extrapolating; extrapolating goes beyond the data.

apps.academic: A graph can help you extrapolate, but a careful scientist states how far past the data the estimate reaches.
apps.spoken: If you extrapolate from the way he plays now, he'll be on the varsity team next year.
apps.writing: Use extrapolate for a reasoned estimate that goes beyond the evidence you have, and say how sure you are.

cloze.s: If the plant grew two inches a week for three weeks, we can ___ that it will keep growing at about that rate next month.

cloze2.s: Careful scientists do not ___ far beyond their data, because patterns can change outside the range they measured.

misuse.s: She extrapolated by reading aloud the exact numbers that were already printed in the table.
misuse.why: To extrapolate is to estimate beyond the known data; reading printed numbers stays within it.

visual.alt: A line graph with a dotted line extending past the last data point.

words.frame: If I extrapolate from ___, I predict ___.

words.def: To propose an explanation that can be tested, before knowing whether it is true.
words.ex: The class hypothesized that plants near the window would grow taller than plants in the corner.
words.ex2: Before opening the box, Jo hypothesized that the humming sound came from a small motor.
words.nonExample: Saying that you like blue is a preference; nobody can test it, so it is not a hypothesis.

morph.note: The base loses its last two letters before -ize (hypothesis -> hypothes).

apps.academic: A scientist hypothesizes before an experiment and then uses the results to support or reject the idea.
apps.spoken: I hypothesize that the cafeteria line is shorter on Fridays; I'll count and see.
apps.writing: Use hypothesize for an explanation you plan to test; a hypothesis must be able to be proved wrong.

cloze.s: The students ___ that salt would slow the melting of the ice, then set up three bowls to test it.

cloze2.s: Before the road test, the engineers ___ that the new tires would stop faster on wet pavement.

misuse.s: She hypothesized that the plant grew after measuring it every day and finishing the study.
misuse.why: To hypothesize is to propose an idea before testing; she had already finished the study.

visual.alt: A laboratory flask beside a thought bubble with a question mark.

words.def: To describe or outline something clearly and precisely, including its edges or limits.
words.ex: The map delineates the border between the two counties with a thick red line.
words.ex2: In her essay, Kara delineated three causes of the strike and explained how each one differed.
words.nonExample: Giving a vague hint about a topic does not delineate it.

apps.academic: Before you argue, delineate your terms so the reader knows exactly what you mean.
apps.spoken: Can you delineate the steps so we don't miss one?
apps.writing: Use delineate when you set out the boundaries or parts of an idea clearly, not just mention it.

cloze.s: The first paragraph should ___ the problem clearly before the essay proposes any solutions.

cloze2.s: Surveyors used wooden stakes to ___ the exact edges of the new playground.

misuse.s: The author delineated the plan so vaguely that no reader could tell what the steps were.
misuse.why: To delineate is to outline clearly; a vague description does the opposite.

visual.alt: A pencil tracing a border line on a map.

words.frame: I will delineate the problem by ___.

words.def: To express an idea or feeling clearly in words.

senses.def: Able to express ideas clearly and easily in speech or writing.
senses.example: An articulate speaker kept the whole room listening.

words.ex: It took Mia a week to articulate why the ending of the novel made her uneasy.
words.ex2: Please articulate your reasons so that the group can judge them fairly.
words.nonExample: Mumbling a few words and shrugging does not articulate an idea.

apps.academic: A strong thesis articulates the writer's position in one clear sentence.
apps.spoken: I can't quite articulate why, but something about the plan feels wrong.
apps.writing: Use articulate as a verb for putting a thought into clear words; use the adjective for a person who does it well.

cloze.s: In the interview, the champion could barely ___ how proud she felt when she heard her name called.

cloze2.s: A strong thesis lets a writer ___ the main argument in a single sentence.

misuse.s: He articulated his idea by whispering something that nobody could hear and then walking away.
misuse.why: To articulate is to express clearly; whispering unheard words expresses nothing.

visual.alt: A speaker with a speech bubble that holds a lightbulb.

words.frame: I can articulate my idea by saying ___.

words.def: To place something in its setting of time, place, and circumstances so that it can be understood.
words.ex: A museum label contextualizes the vase by explaining who used it and what daily life was like.
words.ex2: Before judging the old law, the class tried to contextualize it by learning what problems the town faced.
words.nonExample: Quoting a sentence while hiding when and why it was said does not contextualize it.

segs.m: relating to the setting around an idea

apps.academic: Historians contextualize a source by asking who made it, when, and for whom before they judge what it says.
apps.spoken: To contextualize the score, remember that half the team was out sick.
apps.writing: Use contextualize when you add the surrounding facts that change how a quote, event, or number should be read.

cloze.s: To ___ the poster, the guide explained that it was printed during a week when the whole city was under snow.

cloze2.s: Historians ___ each speech by checking what events happened just before it was given.

misuse.s: To contextualize the letter, the teacher removed its date, its author, and the place it was sent from.
misuse.why: To contextualize is to add the setting; removing those details takes the setting away.

visual.alt: A framed picture shown inside a larger map.

words.frame: To contextualize this quote, I would explain that ___.

words.def: To place two things side by side so that their similarities or differences become clear.
words.ex: The film juxtaposes shots of a crowded city with shots of an empty field to show loneliness.
words.ex2: In her report, Dana juxtaposed two maps of the town drawn a century apart.
words.nonExample: Describing only one picture in detail does not juxtapose it with anything.

apps.academic: Authors juxtapose two scenes so that readers notice a difference without being told.
apps.spoken: If you juxtapose the two photos, you can see how much the park changed.
apps.writing: Use juxtapose when you deliberately set two items next to each other to reveal a point.

cloze.s: The museum chose to ___ a child's crayon drawing with a master's painting to spark a conversation about what counts as art.

cloze2.s: Writers sometimes ___ a quiet scene and a loud one so that the reader feels the difference.

misuse.s: The artist juxtaposed the two photos by hiding one in a drawer and never showing it.
misuse.why: To juxtapose is to place two things side by side; hiding one prevents any comparison.

visual.alt: Two pictures placed side by side with arrows between them.

words.frame: When I juxtapose ___ and ___, I notice ___.

words.def: To be a clear case of something, or to show it by offering a typical case.
words.ex: The old oak exemplifies how one tree can shelter an entire neighborhood of wildlife.
words.ex2: Ms. Lee's volunteer work at the shelter exemplifies what the club means by service.
words.nonExample: A single unusual case that differs from all the others does not exemplify the group.

apps.academic: A body paragraph should exemplify the claim with one well-chosen detail from the text.
apps.spoken: His patience exemplifies what a good coach should be.
apps.writing: Use exemplify to name the thing that shows a quality clearly, then explain how it does so.

cloze.s: The story of the lighthouse keeper's patience ___ the quality the author calls endurance.

cloze2.s: Her careful, step-by-step solution ___ the kind of clear reasoning the teacher wanted to see.

misuse.s: The messy desk exemplifies how tidy and well organized its owner is.
misuse.why: To exemplify is to be a clear case of something; a messy desk is a case of disorder.

visual.alt: A medal pinned next to a model sample.

passage.title: What Happened at the Pond
paras: When the fish in the school pond died overnight, Ms. Brandt's science class had one week to write an investigation report. Her prompt used a verb that was new to most of the class: "Synthesize what the sources tell us about the cause." Tomas groaned. "Does that mean summarize?" "No," she said. "It means combine them into one new understanding."

The sources were a water-quality chart, the custodian's log, and a weather report. Amira began by delineating the problem on the board: which fish had died, on which day, and under what conditions. Then she postulated that a sudden drop in temperature had stressed the fish. "Good," said Ms. Brandt, "but a postulate is only a starting point. Turn it into something we can hypothesize and test." When the class checked the weather report, they found that the night had been mild, so the cold-weather idea had to go.

Tomas studied the chart. It listed oxygen readings for five days, and each reading was lower than the one before. "If I extrapolate the pattern," he said, "the oxygen would have been too low by Tuesday night." The custodian's log corroborated his idea: it noted that the pond's fountain pump had stopped on Tuesday afternoon.

Ms. Brandt asked Priya to contextualize the readings. Priya juxtaposed two charts, one from August and one from the week of the fish kill, and the difference was easy to see. In August the oxygen level stayed steady even on hot days, so the low readings that week were unusual.

For the last step, Amira had to articulate her claim in two sentences: "The fish most likely died because the pump stopped and the oxygen dropped. Three sources point to the same cause." Ms. Brandt wrote a note beside it: "This paragraph exemplifies the writing I want: a claim, evidence from more than one source, and a careful limit."

qs.q: In paragraph 1, Ms. Brandt tells the class to "synthesize" the sources. She means that students should
choices: copy the best source and cite it
combine the sources into one new explanation
choose the source they trust most
retell each source in order
qs.why: She answers Tomas's question about summarizing by saying it means combining the sources into one new understanding.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Brandt say that a postulate is "only a starting point"?
choices: She thinks Amira's idea is foolish.
She wants the class to ignore the weather report.
She does not want anyone to guess about the pond.
She wants the class to test the idea before treating it as true.
qs.why: Ms. Brandt asks Amira to turn the postulate into something the class can test, and the weather report then shows it was wrong.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the custodian's log corroborated Tomas's prediction?
choices: The log recorded that the pond's pump stopped on Tuesday afternoon.
The log was kept by a custodian.
The log appeared next to the weather report.
The log listed five days of oxygen readings.
qs.why: Tomas predicted that oxygen would be too low by Tuesday night, and a pump that stopped Tuesday afternoon supports that timing.

qs.q: What does Priya's juxtaposition of the two charts show the class?
choices: The pond is cleaner in August than in any other month.
The low oxygen readings that week were unusual compared with August.
The custodian was wrong about the pump.
The weather report was missing information.
qs.why: She places August beside the week of the fish kill and finds that August stayed steady while that week did not.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: Fountains are the most important part of a school pond.
A good explanation comes from testing ideas and combining several sources.
Students should never trust a weather report.
The first idea someone proposes is usually correct.
qs.why: The class tests a postulate, rejects it, uses a chart, a log, and a comparison, and then combines them into one explanation.

write.prompt: Choose a question you would like to investigate, such as why a plant grows or why a bus runs late. Explain how you would hypothesize, find a corroborating source, and synthesize what you learn, using at least three words from this unit.
write.frame: I would hypothesize that ___. A source that could corroborate it is ___. I would synthesize the evidence by ___.

study.task: Sort the ten words by their endings. Choose one word from each group and explain how the ending signals that the word is a verb. Then turn one verb into a noun, as in hypothesize to hypothesis or synthesize to synthesis, and use both forms in a sentence.

shades.label: how much evidence stands behind an idea

choices: predict : check
write : paper
cold : frozen
doctor : patient
contradict : oppose
teach : classroom
hot : cold
pen : ink

sentences: Write a sentence about a question you could hypothesize about at school. Say what you would test.
Write a sentence that uses both corroborate and contextualize to describe how you would check a rumor.
Write a sentence about two things you would juxtapose to show a change over time.
Write a sentence that shows you can articulate a feeling that is hard to name.

given: The border runs between two counties.
The line is thick and red.
combine.model: The map delineates the border between two counties with a thick red line.

given: The first witness told what happened.
A second witness told the same story.
The two witnesses did not know each other.
combine.model: A second witness who did not know the first corroborated the story of what happened.

discuss: What is the difference between a hypothesis and a postulate? Use both words.
When is it risky to extrapolate from a small amount of data? Explain with extrapolate and one other word from the unit.
Which task verb from this unit would be most useful on a history essay, and why?
produce.explain: Explain how synthesizing is different from summarizing. Use synthesize and give one example with two sources.

argue.prompt: Claim: A report should always corroborate a surprising claim with at least two independent sources before it is published. Take a side and support it with two reasons using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. A single source could ___, but a corroborated claim would ___.

constructed.prompt: A student says that the library is quietest on Wednesdays. Use hypothesize and corroborate to explain how she could test the idea.
look: names a second source or kind of evidence that could corroborate it
constructed.model: She could hypothesize that Wednesdays are the quietest by counting noise levels each day for a month. A librarian's attendance log could corroborate her counts.

constructed.prompt: A poster from 1950 and a poster from today advertise the same product. Use juxtapose, contextualize, and articulate to explain what you would do with them in a history essay.
look: places the posters side by side
adds the time and setting before judging, then states a clear claim
constructed.model: I would juxtapose the two posters to see what changed. Then I would contextualize each one by noting when it was made and who it was made for. Finally I would articulate a claim about how advertising reflects its time.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten task verbs for working with evidence, read a short narrative about a class investigating a school pond, practice the verb endings -ize, -ate, and -ify, and write a plan for investigating a question. The aim is that a student who sees one of these verbs in a prompt can name the thinking that it requires.

notes.va.synthesize.v: Synthesize means to combine sources into a new understanding. It differs from summarize because it creates a claim no single source states. Have students do a two-source synthesis and then check whether their sentence could have been copied from one source alone.
notes.va.postulate.v: Postulate is a starting assumption, put forward before proof. It is often confused with prove and with predict. Use an everyday starting assumption ('I postulate the bus is late because of rain') and then ask what test would turn it into a hypothesis.
notes.va.corroborate.v: Corroborate needs a second, independent source. Two classmates who copied each other do not corroborate each other. Practice with an eyewitness scenario. Link to qualify from unit 1: weak corroboration calls for a qualified claim.
notes.va.extrapolate.v: Extrapolate means to extend a pattern beyond the data. Use a simple graph with a dotted line. Discuss the risk: the further you go, the less certain you can be. Avoid using it for any guess; it must rest on a pattern.
notes.va.hypothesize.v: Hypothesize is for explanations that can be tested. Remind students that a good hypothesis can be proved wrong. Model the suffix: hypothesis + -ize. Distinguish from postulate: hypotheses are set up for testing; postulates may serve as assumptions inside a theory.
notes.va.delineate.v: Delineate is to set out clearly and precisely, often boundaries or parts. It sounds fancy but works for maps, rules, and essay terms. Have students delineate 'fair' in a school rule. English learners may need the cognate delinear.
notes.va.articulate.v: Articulate is a verb here (ar-TIK-yuh-late) and an adjective in another pronunciation (ar-TIK-yuh-lit). Teach the verb and mention the adjective. Students who struggle to articulate an idea can first speak it to a partner.
notes.va.contextualize.v: Contextualize means add the surrounding facts. Model with a quotation: show it alone, then with the date, speaker, and audience. Link to the history units to come. The word has a base, contextual, plus -ize.
notes.va.juxtapose.v: Juxtapose is to put side by side so a point shows. The point matters: juxtaposing without drawing a conclusion is only listing. Use two photographs. Spelling and pronunciation are hard; give students a chant for the x.
notes.va.exemplify.v: Exemplify means to be a clear case of something, or to show something by giving a case. Students often use it to mean 'be an example of anything.' Ask them to prove the match: 'how does this case show the quality?' The family includes example and exemplary.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The prompt says synthesize. That tells me not to summarize each source one at a time. I will look for a claim that the chart, the log, and the weather report all support. The chart shows falling oxygen, the log says the pump stopped, and the weather report rules out cold, so I can articulate one claim that uses all three.'
discuss: Which task verb from this unit is the hardest to do well, and why?
What is the difference between disagreeing with a source and corroborating a different claim?
misconceptions: A hypothesis is just a guess.
Corroborate means to repeat the same claim.
Extrapolate can be used for any prediction, even with no data.
extend: Choose a school routine and write a three-sentence investigation plan using hypothesize, corroborate, and extrapolate.
Find two sources about the same event and write a one-paragraph synthesis that uses juxtapose and contextualize.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit these verbs within two days by attaching one to every constructed-response prompt in other classes, and at one week by asking students to say which verb a prompt requires. The unit 1 word qualify returns when students limit a synthesis claim, and inherent, slant, and skew return when they judge a source's reliability.

frames: A second source that could corroborate this is ___.
To contextualize the quote, I would explain ___.
If I extrapolate from ___, I predict ___.
wida.oral: Partner A reads a prompt that contains one task verb from the unit. Partner B says what the prompt is asking the writer to do, in their own words, and names one step.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: sintetizar, postular, corroborar, extrapolar, plantear como hipótesis (a phrase; hipotetizar is rare), delinear, articular, contextualizar, yuxtaponer, ejemplificar.
Cognate flags for the -ar verbs should be confirmed.

Sense boundary: postulate and hypothesize are separated only by testability; confirm that grade 8 readers can separate them. Articulate is taught as a verb; the adjective sense appears as a second sense.
Morphology: hypothesize is shown as hypothesis plus -ize with a documented respelling; no further etymology is claimed.
